# Agent-created custom services

## Overview

- Today a "custom service" (one detent has no schemas for) is hand-written package data: `libs/mngr_latchkey/imbue/mngr_latchkey/additional_services.json` holds exactly one entry, `claude-ai`, and shipping another one means editing the repo, regenerating `extensions/services.json`, and cutting a release. Give agents a way to ask for one at runtime instead: an agent names a domain and a rationale, the user approves once, and the connection exists from then on like any catalog service.
- The request and the grant are a **single** permission request. A new `custom-service` request type in the gateway's `permission_requests` extension carries the domain plus an optional cookie login flow; approving it registers the service *and* grants the agent access to it in one user action.
- The scope structure is fixed: one scope schema pinning `domain` to a `const`, granted with detent's builtin catch-all permission `any`. A custom service defines **no permission schema of its own** -- `any` is a builtin every scope implicitly admits (`store.py:353`'s admin config already relies on it, and minds never sets `permissionsDoNotUseBuiltinSchemas`), so the only schema a custom service defines is its scope. This differs from `claude-ai`, whose hand-written `everything` permission with body `{}` is exactly `any` under another name; `everything` stays claude-ai's alone rather than becoming a name every custom service redefines. The only things an agent gets to choose are the domain and whether there is a cookie login.
- **The grant is self-contained.** The approval effect carries both the scope schema (the domain `const`) and the account-gated schema that `$ref`s it, so approving writes everything the host's `permissions.json` needs into that one file. Nothing is added to `minds_shared_schemas.json`, which means this is unaffected by [#605](https://github.com/imbue-ai/mngr-internal/pull/605) inlining the bundled schemas and deleting that file and its `include` -- the design works identically before and after it lands, and needs no rework either way.
- Note the two different `any`s: the grant is `{"<derived-scope>": ["any"]}`, which is the catch-all *permission* under a scope pinned to one domain. Detent's wildcard *scope* is also spelled `any`, and a rule keyed `any` authorizes every service -- that is the admin grant, and a custom service must never produce one.
- **The agent supplies no display text.** A custom service is labelled by its domain everywhere it is named -- the request dialog, the Permissions tab, the Connectors page -- because the domain is the one string that cannot misdescribe what the connection reaches. The agent's rationale stays the only agent-authored text on screen, and it is already presented as the agent's own words under a **Reason** heading rather than as the app's description of the service.
- The service catalog gains one assembly layer with three sources -- detent builtins, minds' bundled additional services, and user-created ones -- replacing today's split where the first two are folded together at build time by a script. That refactor is behavior-preserving, worth landing on its own, and is what keeps the feature from having to merge a second catalog in each of two languages. See "Making the change small" below.
- The service catalog stops being purely static. `ServicesCatalog` gains a user-created layer, which is what makes a custom service appear in the permission dialog, the Permissions tab's "Add connection" list, the Connectors page, and the VPS credential sync -- all five surfaces already go through that one class.
- **That layer needs no new file: latchkey's own `config.json` is the store.** A custom service has to be written into `registeredServices` regardless, or no gateway can resolve a request to it -- and everything else about it is derivable from that entry. The `custom_` prefix says which entries are ours; the domain is the host of `baseApiUrl`; the display name is the domain; the scope schema is that domain as a `const`; there are no per-service permissions, since the grant uses builtin `any`. A parallel `custom_services.json` would hold a second copy of all of it, with the usual consequence that the two can disagree. (The bundled `additional_services.json` stays a file because it is package data shipped in the wheel, which `config.json` cannot be.)
- Nothing is lost by dropping the sidecar, including provenance: which agent asked for a service and when is already recorded, as the permission request and its response event in `~/.minds/events/requests/events.jsonl`.
- **This work depends on an unreleased latchkey.** Through 3.8.0, `registeredServices` is loaded into a module-level registry once at CLI start, so a running gateway never sees a new registration -- and since `latchkey auth browser` is executed *by the gateway process*, the cookie sign-in could not even run until the gateway was restarted. The latchkey `refresh-services` branch rebuilds the registry (and rereads the whole config) per request, which removes that entirely: a registration written to `config.json` is live on the next request, `auth browser` included. Verified against a local build of that branch -- a gateway that had already answered `Unknown service` for a name answered with its full `services info`, `authOptions: ["browser", "set"]`, after nothing but a `config.json` write. The released 3.3.0 still answers `Unknown service` under the same test. **Do not merge this before that latchkey ships**, and bump the four version pins (the `bump-latchkey` skill) to the release that carries it.
- One constraint from latchkey remains and is not negotiable without a further upstream change: a registered service with no stored credentials is a hard 400 (`NoCredentialsForServiceError`; minds does not set `passthroughUnknown`). "No cookie flow" therefore means "the user pastes a token", not "unauthenticated access to a domain": a domain with genuinely no auth stays unsupported. This needs no new UI -- `RegisteredService.setCredentialsExample` already returns `latchkey auth set <name> -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>"`, which `credential_commands.py` already renders as a labelled form.

## Expected behavior

The agent's side:

- An agent that needs a domain latchkey does not know about POSTs `{"type": "custom-service", "rationale": "...", "payload": {...}}` to the gateway's `permission-requests` extension, then ends its turn -- the same contract as every other request type, and already covered by the agent baseline's `POST /permission-requests` grant.
- The payload is `{"domain": "example.com", "login": {"login_url": ..., "cookie_url": ..., "cookie_keys": [...]}}`. `domain` is required and `login` is optional; there is no third field. `ensureNoExtraneousFields` already rejects anything else, so an agent that tries to smuggle a label in gets an HTTP 400 rather than having it quietly ignored.
- **The payload names a domain, not a `baseApiUrl`, even though a `baseApiUrl` is what latchkey stores.** The registration's is synthesized as `https://<domain>/`. The two are not interchangeable: latchkey picks a service by `url.startsWith(baseApiUrl)` (`serviceRegistry.js`, `matchesUrl`), while detent matches the scope on `domain`, which it computes as `url.hostname.toLowerCase()` (`decomposedRequest.js:51`) -- bare hostname, no port. A bare origin is the only `baseApiUrl` for which those two agree, so it is the only one worth accepting:
  - a **port** (`https://example.com:8443/`) narrows latchkey's matching but is invisible to detent, so a scope pinning `example.com:8443` never matches and one pinning `example.com` also admits port 443;
  - a **path** (`https://example.com/v1/`) injects credentials only under `/v1/` while the scope's `domain` const covers the whole host, so the grant is broader than the injection -- and two such services on one host produce two scopes matching the same `domain`, where detent stops at the first matching rule.

  Taking a domain and synthesizing the origin makes all of that unrepresentable rather than merely discouraged, and keeps one custom service per host. A path-scoped custom service is not expressible, which costs nothing: the fixed single-`domain` scope could not have expressed one anyway.
- The accepted `domain` grammar is deliberately narrow, because the name derivation below depends on it: ASCII only, lowercased before validation, at least two labels, at most 253 characters, each label 1-63 characters of `[a-z0-9]` and `-` with neither a leading nor a trailing `-`. In particular **no underscore** -- which is also simply correct, since an RFC 1123 hostname label is letters, digits and hyphens. A non-ASCII domain is rejected with "supply the punycode (A-label) form"; `xn--` labels are themselves letters-digits-hyphens, so an internationalized domain maps through the rest of this unchanged.
- The extension also rejects, with a message the agent can act on: a `domain` carrying a scheme, port, path, userinfo or wildcard; an IP literal, `localhost`, or a reserved suffix (so nothing can shadow `latchkey-self.invalid`); a `login_url`/`cookie_url` that is not `https://` on the domain itself or a subdomain of it; an empty or oversized `cookie_keys`; and a domain **any** catalog scope already covers -- not merely one whose derived name is taken. The check is on the domain rather than the name because the bundled services do not carry the `custom_` prefix: `claude.ai` derives `custom_claude_ai`, which collides with nothing by name, yet its scope would pin the same `domain` const as the shipped `claude-ai` scope. Two rules matching one domain is precisely the case where detent stops at the first and the second silently does nothing. The rejection names the existing scope and tells the agent to send an ordinary `predefined` request for it, so a second agent asking for an already-served domain self-corrects without bothering the user.
- The latchkey service name is `custom_` + the domain with every `.` replaced by `_`: `example.com` -> `custom_example_com`, `a-b.com` -> `custom_a-b_com`, `a.b.com` -> `custom_a_b_com`. Latchkey's name alphabet is `^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]*$` (`serviceRegistry.js`), which admits no `.`, so some substitution is forced.
- **The requirement on that substitution is injectivity, not reversibility.** Two domains must never produce one name -- which the obvious `.` -> `-` fails, mapping `a-b.com` and `a.b.com` both to `a-b-com`. Substituting `_` satisfies it for a plain reason: the domain grammar above admits no `_`, so the substitution is one-to-one on each character and therefore on the whole string. Forbidding `_` in the domain is what buys that, making it a load-bearing rule rather than incidental strictness, and is what the test pins.
- **Nothing ever decodes a name back to a domain, and nothing should.** The domain is recovered from the registration's `baseApiUrl` (`https://example.com/` -> `example.com`) -- parsing a URL, which is what URLs are for, rather than reverse-engineering an identifier. Everything else follows from there or is a lookup: the label and the scope schema's `const` are the domain, and a rule key in a `permissions.json` resolves through `ServicesCatalog.get_by_scope`. A scope whose service no longer exists is already skipped as a non-catalog scope rather than guessed at. So no inverse is written, and the name only has to be injective and legible.
- The `custom_` prefix reserves a namespace no latchkey builtin occupies -- every one of the thirty builtins is a plain name (`slack`, `google-gmail`, ...), and none carries an underscore at all -- so a custom service cannot collide with what latchkey ships today or, by convention, with what it ships later. That convention is the one thing here minds cannot enforce: latchkey's loader silently *skips* a registration whose name a builtin already holds, so a future builtin named `custom_*` would quietly disable an existing custom service rather than erroring. The merge layer already holds both sets, so it checks at startup and surfaces such a service as broken instead of leaving it silently dead. (The check is against the live registry rather than the bundled catalog, since `HIDDEN_BUILTIN_SERVICES` are in the former and absent from the latter.)
- The derived name never appears in the UI -- the domain is the label everywhere -- so its readability matters only for someone reading `config.json` or a `permissions.json` rule key by eye, which is exactly what the `_`-for-`.` choice preserves.

The user's side:

- **The same popup, one more kind.** There is a single review surface (`#request-popup`, fed by `InboxPage`), and `requestDetailView` switches on `detail.kind` to pick a body. A custom-service request adds one `case` arm and one view file, exactly as the `accounts` kind did. Every existing way in -- the chat card's "Review & respond", the Permissions tab's "Waiting on you" row, the titlebar bell, its toasts, an OS notification -- already leads to that popup, so none of them changes.
- **The same chrome.** `PermissionsShell` supplies the marked header, the optional Account section, **Reason**, the credential form, the Deny / Approve row, and the progress and error notices. A kind supplies only `headerLabel`, `mark`, `rationale`, `progressLabel`, `body`, and optionally `account` and `approveLabel`.
- **The custom-service body is the simplest of the five.** `headerLabel` is the domain; `mark` is the globe glyph; `body` is one sentence saying that approving creates a connection to that domain and lets this workspace use it, plus the login URL when there is a cookie flow. `approveLabel` becomes "Sign in & approve" for a cookie flow, matching what `predefined` already does for a first connection.
- **No account picker, by construction.** The service is being created, so it has no accounts to choose between -- `predefined`'s picker renders nothing in exactly that situation today. The `account` slot is simply left out. A *later* grant to the same service is an ordinary `predefined` request, which has the picker.
- **No permission editor and no "Adjust" link**: the grant is a single `any` permission, so there is nothing to narrow.
- **The no-login case needs no new UI at all.** The credential form lives in `PermissionsShell`, driven by `model.manualCredentialsPrompt()`; `RegisteredService.setCredentialsExample` returns `latchkey auth set <name> -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>"`, and `credential_commands.py` already turns that into one labelled input. The typed-value-is-malformed and typed-value-is-wrong paths, with the reason shown as an error `Notice` scrolled into view, come along unchanged.
- Every string the dialog presents as fact is either the domain, a URL derived from it, or fixed app copy. The agent cannot name the service, so it cannot present `evil-tracker.example` as "Google Drive"; the worst it can do is write a misleading rationale, which reads as the agent's claim and not the app's.
- Approve is a multi-step operation and reads as one: the service is registered, the account is connected (browser sign-in or the typed credentials), and the grant is written. A failure at any step leaves the request **pending** with no response event, and the dialog shows the reason -- the same "a failed approval is never recorded as a denial" contract `predefined` already has, inherited from the shell rather than reimplemented.
- Deny deletes the pending request and writes a `DENIED` response event. Nothing is registered, and no trace of the proposed service is left behind.
- Once created, a custom service is an ordinary connection: it appears in the Permissions tab's left nav and "Add connection" list, on the Connectors page with its account, and its single toggle can be flipped or revoked there. That toggle needs one cosmetic fix: `group_permissions_by_area` sends `any` to a trailing "Extras" group labelled "Everything (unrestricted)", which is right for a service with a dozen specific permissions and reads oddly for one whose only permission is that. A scope whose sole available permission is `any` renders it as a plain full-access row instead of behind an Extras divider. Another workspace gets access through a normal `predefined` request for its scope. Revoking every grant does not unregister the service.
- A custom service has no vendor artwork, so it gets a generic globe mark wherever a service mark is drawn, rather than the `box` glyph that currently stands in for a missing icon.

Propagation:

- The desktop gateway needs no bounce: writing the registration into `config.json` is the whole of it, and the next request through the gateway sees it. Nothing is torn down, no in-flight agent request fails, and no port changes.
- Every provisioned VPS gateway gets the new registration and the host's credentials -- again with no restart. The scope schema needs no shipping of its own: it is inlined in the host's `permissions.json`, which `sync_permissions` already copies. Registration currently only reaches a VPS during `provision_remote_gateway` at discovery, so an already-provisioned host would otherwise hold the credentials and never be able to use them.
- A workspace created *after* the service exists needs nothing special: the registration is in `config.json` and the schema is in the shared file, both of which every gateway reads.

## Making the change small: one catalog overlay

The generator's own comment states the invariant worth keeping:

> Folding them in here means every reader of the catalog -- the Python `ServicesCatalog` and both gateway extensions -- sees exactly one file in one shape, instead of each merging a second file itself.

Custom services cannot be folded at build time, so something has to happen at runtime. The risk is doing it *more than once*: `ServicesCatalog` reads the package resource while the gateway extensions read a materialized copy, so the obvious implementation merges twice, in two languages, feeding the two hand-written catalog parsers in the `.mjs` files.

So there is exactly **one overlay function** and every consumer goes through it:

- `custom_services.py` projects the `custom_`-prefixed entries of latchkey's `config.json` into catalog entries in the shape `services.json` already uses.
- `ServicesCatalog` serves the shipped `services.json` with that overlay applied.
- `_materialize_bundled_extensions` writes `extensions/services.json` as the *same* overlaid catalog, so the gateway extensions keep reading one file in one shape and **do not change at all**. Their duplicated parsers stay out of the blast radius.

Nothing else needs a source of custom services. The registration is already in `config.json`, so `merge_minds_latchkey_config` stays bundled-only. The scope schema rides in the approval effect, so no schemas file is involved. That leaves one function and two callers, which is the whole of the catalog-side work.

## What this does to the bundled `claude-ai`

Nothing at all -- it is left exactly as it is, and that is the whole migration story.

It is tempting to convert it into a custom service now that the machinery exists, and it is not safe. Doing so would rename it (`claude-ai` -> `custom_claude_ai`), rename its scope, replace its `everything` permission with `any`, and replace its curated "Claude" label and brand mark with the domain and a globe. Hosts in the field carry a rule keyed `claude-ai:<account>` whose schema `$ref`s `#/$defs/claude-ai` and whose permission list names `everything`; renaming those is a rename of things live rules point at, and stored credentials are keyed by service name, so it would orphan the login too.

So the bundled mechanism is not superseded in the sense of being removed. What it loses is its monopoly: it stops being the only way, and stops being the default way, to reach a service detent has no schemas for. A new one no longer needs a repo edit, a regenerated catalog and a release. `additional_services.json` keeps `claude-ai` and earns new entries only when a service wants something a derived one cannot have -- a curated display name, a brand mark, a specific cookie-key list.

**Existing workspaces need no migration and get no data-format step.** Nothing about the bundled path changes: the generator still folds `claude-ai` into `services.json`, `additional_services.py` still supplies its schemas and its registration, and its rules, credentials and VPS state are untouched. The only new thing in the system is an overlay that adds entries and removes none.

## Changes

`libs/mngr_latchkey`:

- New `custom_services.py`: pure derivation, no storage. It owns the accepted domain grammar, the name derivation from a domain (one direction only -- see above), the registration entry built from `(domain, login)`, and the projection of a `registeredServices` block into catalog entries -- keeping only `custom_`-prefixed keys, and reading each one's domain off its `baseApiUrl` as the URL's *hostname*, the same thing detent matches on, so a hand-edited entry that grew a port or a path still resolves to the domain the permission check will actually see. An entry whose `baseApiUrl` is absent or has no host is skipped with a warning rather than failing the whole catalog: `config.json` is hand-editable, so one bad entry must not take the rest down. The domain grammar and the name derivation are mirrored in the gateway extension, which validates a request before minds ever sees it; an alignment test pins the two, in the same shape as the existing `account_scopes_test.py` cross-language guard.
- `services_catalog.py`: `ServicesCatalog` applies the overlay on load. The shipped half stays `@cache`d; the overlay is read fresh from `config.json`, so no instance anywhere needs invalidating and a service is visible the moment it is registered.
- `core.py`: `_materialize_bundled_extensions` writes the overlaid catalog into `extensions/services.json` instead of copying the package resource, so the extensions validate against what the desktop sees. `merge_minds_latchkey_config` gains an explicit *preserve* invariant: it already starts from the existing `registeredServices` dict and `update`s only the names minds owns, so `custom_*` keys survive today by construction -- but that is now load-bearing rather than incidental, and gets a test saying so.
- `remote_gateway.py`: a `sync_service_registrations(host, ...)` step that re-runs `_ensure_remote_latchkey_config` with the desktop's `custom_*` entries merged in, called from the new handler and folded into the existing permissions-change sync path in `discovery.py` so a host that was offline catches up. No schemas shipping and no remote gateway restart.
- `README.md`: document the `custom_` convention in `registeredServices`, the overlay, the per-request registry reload it relies on, and the credentials requirement.

`libs/mngr_latchkey/imbue/mngr_latchkey/extensions/permission_requests.mjs` (the gateway extension):

- New `custom-service` request type: payload validation (domain grammar, URL-within-domain, cookie keys, and non-collision with any catalog scope already pinning that domain), and an effect computed the way `predefined` computes one for an unknown account -- **empty** at creation, because the account does not exist until the user signs in, so the grant can only be applied through an approve override that names it.
- The approve override for a `custom-service` request is `{"account": "..."}`, recomputing a **self-contained** effect: `schemas` carries both the scope schema (the domain `const`) and the account-gated schema that `$ref`s it, and `rules` grants `any` under that key. Approving therefore writes everything the target file needs into the target file. Unlike `predefined` it does not consult the catalog -- the scope is not in the extension's `services.json` at request time, and the scope and permission are fixed by construction.
- The extension registers nothing: registration is a `config.json` write outside the extension's permitted root, so the desktop handler performs it before calling `/approve`. Because the effect is self-contained there is no ordering requirement between the two for schema resolution -- the order is about the sign-in needing a registered service, not about the `$ref`.

`apps/minds` (desktop client and SPA):

- `request_events.py`: `RequestType.CUSTOM_SERVICE_PERMISSION` and `LatchkeyCustomServicePermissionRequestEvent` (domain, login flow, rationale -- no label field anywhere on the event), plus its branch in the event-parsing dispatch.
- `latchkey/gateway_client.py` + `latchkey/permission_requests_consumer.py`: `CustomServiceRequestPayload` and its arm of `streamed_request_to_event`.
- `request_handler.py`: `UiCustomServicePermissionDetail` in the `RequestDetailPayload` union (the SPA's `generated/ui.ts` follows automatically).
- New `latchkey/handlers/custom_service.py`, shaped like the `accounts.py` sibling but with the `predefined.py` credential machinery reused for the connect step. Approve, in order: re-validate the payload against the *current* catalog (another approval may have taken the name); read-merge the registration into `config.json`; rewrite the extension `services.json` from the result; connect the account (browser cookie-capture, or the typed credentials through `build_credential_command_argv`); `POST /approve` with the chosen account; write the response event and `mngr message` the agent; kick the remote sync. Any failure before the last two steps leaves the request pending.
- `latchkey/permission_toggles.py`: render `any` as a plain full-access row (not under the Extras divider) when it is a scope's only available permission. `permission_overview.py` already labels a granted `any` as "all" with an unrestricted-access description, so the Connectors page needs nothing.
- `cli/run.py`: construct and register the new handler alongside the other four.
- `electron/paths.js` (already landed, for development against an unreleased latchkey): `getLatchkeyPath()` honors `MINDS_LATCHKEY_BINARY` **in dev mode only**, so the app can be run against a latchkey checkout. The var already exists and `minds run` already reads it; the shell was overwriting it unconditionally with the bundled path. A packaged build ignores it, mirroring `getMindsRootName`, so a stale export from a parent shell cannot redirect a shipped binary.
- SPA: `views/pages/inbox/CustomServicePermissionDetail.ts` -- a single `PermissionsShell` call with `headerLabel`, `mark`, `rationale`, `progressLabel`, `body` and an `approveLabel`, no `account` slot -- plus its `case` arm in `RequestDetail.ts` and its `kind` in the `InboxDetail` union. `ServiceMark.ts` gains a globe fallback for services with no artwork on disk, replacing the `box` glyph in the nav and catalog fallbacks in `PermissionsTab.ts`.
- `docs/latchkey-permissions.md`: the new request type, the approve sequence, and the credentials requirement -- including the explicit statement that a domain with no auth at all is not supported.

`default-workspace-template` (separate repo, worked via `.external_worktrees/`):

- The latchkey skill learns the `custom-service` request type: when to use it (a domain latchkey has no service for) versus a `predefined` request (the service already exists, including one a previous agent created), the payload shape, and the fact that the connection needs credentials -- so the agent's rationale tells the user what they are about to be asked to paste or sign into.

Tests:

- `custom_services.py`: a registration synthesizing `https://<domain>/` and nothing else (a port or path in an accepted domain would be a validation hole), the name derivation being injective over a corpus of near-miss domains (with `a-b.com` / `a.b.com` -- the pair `.` -> `-` would have collided -- as the headline case), an underscore in the domain being rejected as the precondition the injectivity argument rests on, the collision rules, the catalog projection, a `custom_` entry with a missing or hostless `baseApiUrl` being skipped rather than taking the catalog down, and a non-`custom_` registration (a user's own `latchkey services register`) not being mistaken for one of ours.
- The bundled `claude-ai` surviving intact: the overlay adds entries and removes none, the catalog still serves the curated "Claude" display name, and a `custom-service` request for `claude.ai` is refused as already covered rather than creating a second scope on that domain.
- `core_test.py`: `merge_minds_latchkey_config` preserving `custom_*` entries verbatim across a re-merge -- the invariant that makes `config.json` usable as the store.
- `permission_requests_test.py`: the full validation matrix (bad domains, off-domain URLs, reserved names, builtin collisions, already-created service), a payload carrying any label-ish extra field being rejected rather than ignored, the empty-at-creation effect, and the account override recomputation.
- A test pinning that the projected `display_name` equals the domain, and that no field on the request event, the detail payload, or the registration carries agent-authored display text.
- `services_catalog_test.py`: a custom service reaching `get`, `get_by_scope`, `as_mapping`, and `services_for_permissions` (the last one is what ships its credentials to a VPS).
- `handlers/custom_service_test.py`: the approve ordering (register before approve), the pending-on-failure contract at each step, and deny leaving nothing behind.
- `remote_gateway_test.py`: a custom service's registration reaching an already-provisioned VPS's config.
- An acceptance test over a live gateway: register a custom service, then reach it on the next request with no restart. This is the one assumption the whole design rests on, and it lives upstream, so it is worth pinning here rather than trusting the version floor alone.
- Behaviors: entries in `apps/minds/behaviors/` for the user-visible invariants -- a custom service becomes an ordinary connection, a failed approval never reads as a denial, a denied request registers nothing.

## Testing against an unreleased latchkey

Until the reload lands in a release, development runs against a latchkey checkout.

1. Build it: `npm run build` in the latchkey worktree, then `chmod +x dist/src/cli.js` (the build does not set the bit, and the file carries its own `#!/usr/bin/env node`). `dist/` is gitignored, so this leaves the checkout clean.
2. Point minds at it: `export MINDS_LATCHKEY_BINARY=<worktree>/dist/src/cli.js` before launching the app. This reaches everything -- `minds run` passes the path to `LatchkeyForwardSupervisor` as `--latchkey-binary`, which passes it to the detached `mngr latchkey forward`, which spawns the gateway with it.
3. For `mngr latchkey ...` and pytest, the plugin's own chain already covers it: `--latchkey-binary`, else `MNGR_LATCHKEY_BINARY`, else `[plugins.latchkey].latchkey_binary`, else `latchkey` on PATH.

Two things this does not reach. A **VPS** gateway installs latchkey from npm at the pinned `remote_gateway.LATCHKEY_VERSION`, and an **in-workspace** latchkey comes from default-workspace-template's own pin, so neither can run an unpublished build -- local and Docker workspaces are the testable ones until there is a release (or a prerelease published under a dist-tag).

`LATCHKEY_MIN_VERSION` is `3.8.0` and the branch reports `3.8.0`, so the floor does not block the checkout today. Once the reload ships, the floor has to move to that release, or minds will happily accept a latchkey that cannot serve a custom service.

## Risks and things to watch

- **The version floor is load-bearing in a way floors usually are not.** Against a latchkey without the per-request reload, this feature does not degrade -- it silently half-works: the service registers, the catalog shows it, and every request to it fails `Unknown service` until the app is restarted. `LATCHKEY_MIN_VERSION` refuses to initialize below the floor, so the failure is caught, but the four pins must move together (see the `bump-latchkey` skill) or a VPS or in-workspace latchkey lands below it.
- **Do not tidy `claude-ai` onto the derived shape.** Once both kinds of service exist side by side, normalizing the odd one out is a natural-looking cleanup: rewrite `everything` to `any`, or `display_name` to the domain. It is not safe -- host files in the field name `everything` and `$ref` `#/$defs/claude-ai`, and stored credentials are keyed by service name. Leave it alone.
- **A domain is claimed once and kept.** Nothing in this plan lets a user rename or delete a custom service, so a domain created by mistake stays in the catalog and in latchkey's `config.json`. A "remove connection" action on the Connectors page is the follow-up; it has to unregister the service, drop its scope schema, and revoke every host rule naming that scope, so it is real work rather than a one-line deletion.
- **`config.json` becomes an input, not just an output.** minds currently treats a registration as opaque -- it writes the block and deliberately models none of its contents, so a field a later latchkey adds needs no code change here. Reading the custom services back means minds now depends on one field of latchkey's schema, `baseApiUrl`, to recover a domain. That is a small and stable dependency, and the alternative (a second copy of every definition, free to drift from the file that actually drives the gateway) is worse. But it does mean a hand-edit of a `custom_*` entry's `baseApiUrl` silently repoints the scope schema of an existing grant. That is the user's own 0700 data directory, next to the permissions files themselves, so it is not a new trust boundary -- and one source of truth at least moves consistently, where a store-plus-config split would have left the two disagreeing.
- **`passthroughUnknown` remains the only route to a genuinely public API**, and turning it on would change existing services too (a granted service with no credentials would send unauthenticated requests instead of reporting "No credentials found", and passthrough requests carry no account metadata, so account-gated rules could never match them). Left out deliberately; revisit only with an upstream per-service opt-out.
- **A separate, pre-existing bug found while scoping this, now out of scope.** `LatchkeyForwardSupervisor.restart()` spawns a fresh supervisor, which allocates a *new* gateway port (`start_gateway`'s `preferred_port` is only reused within one process). Non-tunneled workspaces have the old port baked into `LATCHKEY_GATEWAY` at create time, so any full restart -- the discovery-health watchdog does one -- silently breaks their gateway URL. This work no longer restarts anything, so it neither causes nor fixes that; it wants its own change, persisting the published `gateway_port` and passing it as `preferred_port` on the first spawn.
